Content:
To plot the graph of a logarithmic function, it helps to remember that the inverse of a logarithmic function is an exponential function. So, we can just plot the exponential function and reflect it over the line [MATH: y=x.]

Content:
For example, suppose that we wish to plot the graph of

Content:
[MATH: y=\log_2 x.]

Content:
The corresponding inverse function is [MATH: y=2^x,] and since [MATH: y=2^x] is a one-to-one function defined for all real [MATH: x,] we can obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\log_2{x}] by reflecting [MATH: y=2^x] over the line [MATH: y=x.] The result is shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/088e8c344ad4154c228565ccb45be85d]

Content:
Here are some key points to note about [MATH: y=\log_2(x)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- The domain is [MATH: x>0], and the range is [MATH: -\infty < y < \infty.]
- The graph has the vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]
- The function is an increasing function.
- The graph passes through the point [MATH: (1,0).]
- For [MATH: x>1], the graph is positive and grows very slowly as we increase [MATH: x.] We say that [MATH: y\rightarrow \infty] (slowly) as [MATH: x\rightarrow \infty.]

Content:
In general, for any base [MATH: n>1,] the graph of [MATH: y=\log_n{x}] always has the same shape, and all of the above points are valid. We can verify that this is true by inspecting some possible graphs shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e49d7b6bf111a94b614897264c1e2317]

Content:
Note: The important points covered above also apply to two familiar logarithms.

Content:
- [MATH: y = \ln x = \log_e x] is the natural logarithm. Since the base is [MATH: n=e>1,] all of the important points covered above apply.
- [MATH: y = \log x = \log_{10} x] is the logarithm with base [MATH: 10.] Since the base is [MATH: n=10>1,] all the important points covered above apply.

  • The function has the vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]

  • The function is an increasing function.

sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function [MATH: y=\ln(x)?]

1. [MATH: y\rightarrow-\infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow 0^+]
2. The curve passes through the point [MATH: (1,0)]
3. [MATH: y\rightarrow\infty] as [MATH: x\rightarrow -\infty]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\ln (x).]

Now, let's consider each statement.

  • Statement I is true. As [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 0^+,] [MATH: y] decreases without bound.

  • Statement II is true. Substituting [MATH: x=1] into the equation of the curve gives a result of [MATH: 0\mathbin{:}] [MATH: y|= \ln (1) = 0✓]

  • Statement III is false. The function is not defined for [MATH: x<0,] so the function is not defined as [MATH: x \to -\infty.]

In conclusion, only statements I and II are true.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To plot the graph of a logarithmic function, it helps to remember that the inverse of a logarithmic function is an exponential function. So, we can just plot the exponential function and reflect it over the line [MATH: y=x.]

Content:
For example, suppose that we wish to plot the graph of

Content:
[MATH: y=\log_2 x.]

Content:
The corresponding inverse function is [MATH: y=2^x,] and since [MATH: y=2^x] is a one-to-one function defined for all real [MATH: x,] we can obtain the graph of [MATH: y=\log_2{x}] by reflecting [MATH: y=2^x] over the line [MATH: y=x.] The result is shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/088e8c344ad4154c228565ccb45be85d]

Content:
Here are some key points to note about [MATH: y=\log_2(x)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- The domain is [MATH: x>0], and the range is [MATH: -\infty < y < \infty.]
- The graph has the vertical asymptote [MATH: x=0.]
- The function is an increasing function.
- The graph passes through the point [MATH: (1,0).]
- For [MATH: x>1], the graph is positive and grows very slowly as we increase [MATH: x.] We say that [MATH: y\rightarrow \infty] (slowly) as [MATH: x\rightarrow \infty.]

Content:
In general, for any base [MATH: n>1,] the graph of [MATH: y=\log_n{x}] always has the same shape, and all of the above points are valid. We can verify that this is true by inspecting some possible graphs shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e49d7b6bf111a94b614897264c1e2317]

Content:
Note: The important points covered above also apply to two familiar logarithms.

Content:
- [MATH: y = \ln x = \log_e x] is the natural logarithm. Since the base is [MATH: n=e>1,] all of the important points covered above apply.
- [MATH: y = \log x = \log_{10} x] is the logarithm with base [MATH: 10.] Since the base is [MATH: n=10>1,] all the important points covered above apply.
